notes.meaning: During the days when Israel had no king, society began to fall into moral disorder. A Levite living in the remote hill country of Ephraim took a concubine from Bethlehem as a secondary wife. While taking a concubine was a common practice in that culture, it fell short of God's original design for marriage.

The woman broke faith with her husband and went back to live in her father's home in Bethlehem. She stayed there for four full months. Some ancient translations suggest she left because of anger and quarreling rather than sexual unfaithfulness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the young woman was not unfaithful or angry, but fled to her father's house to escape mistreatment by the Levite.

notes.meaning: The Levite decided to pursue her, bringing along a servant and two donkeys to speak kindly to her and win back her heart. She brought him into her home, and her father was overjoyed to see him. The father was eager to see the marriage healed and peace restored.

The father-in-law urged the Levite to stay, and he remained there for three days enjoying their food, drink, and hospitality. This warm reception showed how glad the father was to welcome his son-in-law.
On the fourth day, the visitors woke up early to begin the journey home. The father-in-law stepped in and begged the Levite to strengthen himself with food before setting out on the road.
The two men sat down and spent time eating and drinking together. The host then persuaded the Levite to stay another night and enjoy himself.
The Levite stood up to depart, but his host urged him so strongly that he relented. He agreed to spend yet another night under his father-in-law's roof.

On the fifth morning, the Levite rose early to leave, but the father urged him once more to eat first. The meal was dragged out until late afternoon, causing them to lose the best traveling hours of the day.

When the Levite prepared to leave with his concubine and servant, the father pleaded with him again to spend the night. He pointed out that daylight was fading and suggested they start fresh the next morning.

The Levite was unwilling to delay any longer, so he set out late in the day. He traveled about six miles north with his saddled donkeys and his concubine until they came opposite Jebus, which was Jerusalem.
As they approached Jebus, the day was nearly gone and darkness was setting in. The servant suggested that they stop and spend the night in the Jebusite city for safety.
The Levite refused to lodge in a city of foreigners where no Israelites lived. He chose instead to push ahead to Gibeah, expecting to find hospitality and security among his own countrymen.
He urged his group forward, hoping they could reach Gibeah or Ramah before dark. Both towns belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and lay along their route.
They continued their trip, but the sun went down just as they drew near to Gibeah. The arrival of night left them with no choice but to stop there.

They turned off the road to sleep in Gibeah, and the Levite sat down in the open city square. In those days there were few public inns, yet none of the local Benjaminites invited the travelers into their homes.

That evening, an elderly man returned from working in the fields. He was living as a resident foreigner in Gibeah, but he originally came from the hill country of Ephraim, while the townspeople were Benjaminites.
The old man looked up and noticed the traveler sitting stranded in the public square. He approached him kindly and asked where he had come from and where he was going.

The Levite explained that they were traveling from Bethlehem in Judah back to Ephraim, and that he was heading to or served at the house of the Lord. He pointed out with sorrow that no one in the town had offered him shelter.
He made it clear that they would not be a burden to anyone. They carried their own chopped straw and feed for the donkeys, as well as bread and wine for themselves.
The old man greeted the Levite with a blessing of peace and offered to supply all their needs. Knowing the deep wickedness of the town, he warned them not to spend the night out in the open square.
He welcomed the travelers into his home and fed their donkeys. After washing the dust from their feet, they sat down together to eat and drink.

While they were enjoying their meal, wicked men from the town surrounded the house and began beating heavily on the door. They demanded that the host surrender the male visitor so they could sexually assault him, repeating the infamous wickedness of ancient Sodom.
The host went outside and pleaded with the mob not to commit such an outrageous sin. He reminded them that the Levite was an invited guest who rested under the sacred protection of his home.

In great terror, the host offered his own virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine to the crowd instead. While ancient hospitality laws placed extreme weight on protecting guests, sacrificing innocent women was a shocking and shameful compromise.

When the crowd refused the host's plea, the Levite grabbed his concubine and pushed her outside to the mob. The men of Gibeah brutally raped and abused her through the entire night, letting her go only when dawn began to break.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the ancient text frames the crime mainly as an offense against the Levite's honor and property rather than focusing on the woman's personal trauma.

notes.meaning: At daybreak, the abused woman staggered back to the house where her husband was staying. She collapsed at the entrance and lay there until full daylight.
When the Levite opened the doors that morning to resume his journey, he found her lying fallen before the threshold. Her hands were stretched out toward the door where she had collapsed.
The Levite told her to get up so they could go, but she gave no answer because she had died from the horrific abuse. He placed her lifeless body on a donkey and started home in grief and anger.
Upon reaching home, the Levite took a knife and divided her dead body into twelve pieces. He sent one piece to each of the tribes of Israel as a gruesome summons demanding national justice.

The sight of the severed pieces stunned the people, who agreed that no such crime had taken place since Israel left Egypt. They called upon the whole nation to reflect carefully, gather for counsel, and decide what action must be taken.
